subject: Streaming TTFT & chunk cadence — post-demo clarifications and next steps
messages:
From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
To: Samir Patel <samir.patel@finlogic.com>
Cc: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>, Evelyn Hart <evelyn.hart@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-06-20T14:05:00-07:00
Subject: Streaming TTFT & chunk cadence — post-demo clarifications and next steps

Hi Samir — thanks again for today’s demo. Quick recap from our side and a few clarifying questions so we can size the pilot correctly.

Key targets you mentioned on the call (please confirm):
- TTFT (time-to-first-token): p95 <= 150 ms, p99 goal <= 220 ms
- Sustained throughput: ~500 requests/sec (mixed small/batched queries)
- Expected client concurrency: ~80 concurrent browser/mobile connections across three regions (primary traffic in us-east)
- Streaming: you prefer WebSocket for long-lived interactions, but mentioned some clients may be behind strict corporate proxies (possible SSE fallback)
- Chunk cadence: you indicated that UI expects incremental updates roughly every 100–300 ms to keep the UX smooth; we need to pin a cadence range and maximum payload per chunk

Questions for you (so we don’t mis-configure the pilot):
1) Do you want TTFT measured from Redwoods’ public API edge to first token emitted (inclusive of network hop), or only server-side generation time?
2) For streaming transport, is WebSocket the only acceptable option, or do you need SSE as a guaranteed fallback for proxyed environments?
3) Chunk size limit: is the UI OK with variable-size chunks (e.g., initial small meta chunk then larger chunks), or must we enforce a hard byte/token limit per chunk?
4) Any client-side priming or system messages we should bake into the warm cache assumptions (e.g., consistent system prompt per session)?

Next steps I propose:
- You confirm the three items above (TTFT measurement point, primary streaming transport, chunk sizing constraint)
- We stage a 72-hour pilot using a canary model variant with tracing enabled and a small concurrency ramp (we’ll provide suggested ramp schedule)
- Acceptance criteria proposal: p95 TTFT < 150 ms, p99 TTFT < 220 ms; chunk cadence 100–300 ms with no chunk > 1200 tokens (we can tighten if you prefer)

Attached: SLO-proposal-ttft-v1.pdf (draft acceptance criteria and instrumentation checklist) and a tiny stub log from today’s demo.

Thanks — I’ll loop in Dev for technical follow-up once you confirm.

—Kimberly

Subject: Re: Streaming TTFT & chunk cadence — post-demo clarifications and next steps

Thanks Kimberly — great recap. A few clarifications from our side:

1) Measurement point: we care about perceived client latency, so please measure TTFT from our edge (us-east public CDN) to first token arriving at the client. We will provide a simple browser-side probe to validate.
2) Transport: WebSocket is preferred but we absolutely need SSE as an automatic fallback for enterprise customers behind proxies. If SSE introduces a measurable TTFT penalty, flag it — but fallback is mandatory.
3) Chunk sizing: UI prefers frequent small-ish updates to enable progressive rendering. Our designers asked for updates roughly every 120–250 ms; initial chunk can be smaller (20–40 tokens) to render a fast first impression. Maximum per chunk should be around 800 tokens.
4) Priming: we do a small system prompt per session (approx. 12 tokens) plus a short user history snippet. Treat those as constant for cache assumptions.

Acceptance criteria tweak: we can relax p99 to 250 ms as long as p95 stays <= 160 ms for the pilot. This is to account for some mobile network variability.

We’re also concerned about burst behavior — during business hours we might see short spikes to 1k rps for a few minutes. Can you indicate if autoscaling and burst capacity will preserve the TTFT SLOs?

If this looks right I’ll get procurement involved for the pilot paperwork.

Best,
Samir

Head of Engineering — FinLogic

From: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Streaming TTFT & chunk cadence — post-demo clarifications and next steps

Adding a few technical clarifications that will affect the pilot config and acceptance criteria:

- Measurement semantics: we can instrument TTFT both at our edge (time request accepted) and at the model runtime (first token emit). For perceived client TTFT we need your browser probe but we’ll baseline on edge->emit. We’ll publish both metrics.
- Caching: given the small system prompt and repeated session shapes, aggressive prefix/KV caching will help. Recommend enabling prefix cache with a 45s TTL for sessions that show repeated system token patterns.
- Batching and queuing: to hold p95 low at high throughput, we should aim for micro-batching windows of 10–20 ms where possible; continuous batching with immediate flush for single-turn short inputs. There’s a cost/latency trade-off we’ll show in the pilot dashboard.
- Streaming transport implications: WebSocket gives lower head-of-line delay for two-way connections; SSE runs over HTTP/2 in some environments and can add around 10–40 ms at baseline depending on client network/HTTP middleboxes. We’ll instrument both in pilot.
- Chunk cadence and tokenization: using GPT-like tokenization, 20–40 tokens tends to be ~80–160 bytes depending on content. If UI designers want 120–250 ms cadence, we can do that without huge overhead by pacing flushes from the runtime MV. However, for very long responses we’ll recommend sending a small initial chunk (20 tokens) then larger chunks up to 800 tokens. If the client requires strict size caps we can enforce at the gateway.
- Bursts: our Dedicated/Dedicated+burst offering supports short 1k rps spikes with autoscaling; we’ll provide a runway in the pilot config to simulate a 10-minute 1k rps spike and measure TTFT degradation.

Action items for me:
- Prepare a pilot runtime config with two variants: (A) WebSocket-first, SSE fallback; (B) SSE-first (enterprise proxy mode).
- Provide a ramp schedule and an instrumentation plan (traces, synthetic browser probes).
- Add explicit tokenization assumptions and sample payloads to the pilot plan.

—Dev
Dev Patel
Principal Engineer, Serving Runtime | Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Streaming TTFT & chunk cadence — post-demo clarifications and next steps

Thanks Samir — that helps a lot. Summary and proposed pilot plan below so procurement and engineering have a single source of truth: 

Pilot scope (72 hours):
- Canary variant: WebSocket-first with automatic SSE fallback if the client reports proxy blocking; alternate variant SSE-first for a subset of enterprise IPs.
- Instrumentation: edge TTFT, runtime emit TTFT, client probe (you provide), per-chunk timestamps, and percentiles (p50/p95/p99).
- Traffic profile: nominal 500 rps steady-state, one 10-minute simulated spike to 1k rps on day 2 during business hours to validate burst behavior.
- Acceptance criteria for go/no-go: p95 TTFT <= 160 ms and p99 TTFT <= 250 ms (matches your relaxed target). Chunk cadence between 120–250 ms for interactive flows; initial chunk 20–40 tokens, maximum per chunk 800 tokens.
- Autoscaling: we will enable burst headroom and autoscaling policy to protect SLOs; we’ll document expected cold-start behavior and warm pool size.

Next steps:
1) Samir: confirm measurement point (you confirmed browser probe + edge) and approve pilot dates next week (we suggested Tue–Thu).
2) Procurement: I’ll send a short pilot agreement and cost estimate once Samir confirms dates. procurement@finlogic.com is cc’d.
3) Dev: please attach the pilot runtime config and ramp schedule to the HubSpot deal by EOD so Samir can review.

I’ve attached the SLO draft and a small log stub from today’s demo. I’ll set up the 30-minute sync for Tuesday to walk through the instrumentation plan if that works.

Best,
Kimberly
